title: RFK Jr. acts to ease access to unproven peptides despite opposition from FDA scientists
content: The Trump administration on Wednesday acted to ease access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr . Food and Drug Administration scientific staffers had little input on the decision and opposed the changes, according to six people familiar with its development. The draft policy posted online by Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services covers a handful of injectable peptides promoted within the wellness industry for uses such as building muscle, healing injuries and boosting energy. The government will take comments on the measure for two weeks. The document, primarily written by HHS, faced overwhelming pushback among FDA drug staffers who warned it could undermine the agency’s long-standing mission of keeping unproven health products off the U.S. market, according to the people familiar with its development. The people spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations. The policy directs the FDA not to take action against specialty pharmacies that sell a half-dozen wellness peptides, including BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. Under FDA rules, those chemicals would otherwise be considered illegal drugs because they have not gone through the agency’s rigorous review process for safety and effectiveness. According to the newly posted document, Kennedy determined the change “advances patient choice and freedom” while protecting people in the United States from peptides sold online that are often made from unscreened ingredients. Kennedy has called himself a “big fan” of peptides and previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury. Lee Rosebush of the American Academy of Peptide Medicine said in an online post that HHS had taken “a huge step for patient and provider medical freedom.” The group, which is not a medical professional organization, represents people who prescribe or sell peptides. The peptide business has caught the attention of major telehealth providers, including Hims & Hers, which recently announced plans to offer wellness peptides once the government changed its policy. Wall Street analysts estimate the market could be worth more than $2 billion. Some peptides occur naturally in the human body, where they trigger hormones needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss . The chemicals subject to the new policy have not been approved as safe and effective by the FDA. Still, they are promoted for a range of medical uses, including insomnia, anxiety, inflammatory conditions and migraines. Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official, noted that the FDA has approved rigorously tested drugs for all of those conditions. As people “are diverted from those drugs toward this stuff, there will be more unnecessary pain and suffering,” said Lurie, who now leads the nonprofit Center for Science in the Public Interest. He also questioned the timing of the change, days before the midterm election. “This is a wink and nod to the MAHA faithful in the hope that they’ll show up at the polls,” said Lurie, referring to Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement. A spokesperson for HHS said the agency is “confronting the risks of black-market peptides” by giving Americans “a more controlled alternative through licensed U.S. compounders.” It is the latest example of Kennedy reshaping U.S. health policy in the MAHA mold. Some of the biggest figures in that movement sell peptide injections and supplements. The decision is a stark break from FDA efforts to limit the availability of unproven wellness products, including peptides, stem cell therapies and dietary supplements , that make unsupported medical claims. But that approach put the agency at odds with Kennedy, who has publicly endorsed the benefits of all of those products. The policy published Wednesday is a step back from HHS’ original plan, according to two of the people who discussed its development. HHS officials initially wanted the FDA to draft an official regulation that would add BPC-157 and other peptides to a list of drug substances deemed safe for use by compounding pharmacies, specialty businesses that make customized medications. FDA officials warned that the agency’s scientific staffers had major safety concerns and would not support a regulation deeming the peptides safe. HHS officials moved to a different approach that directs the FDA not to enforce its rules against pharmacies that compound the substances. FDA staffers ultimately provided technical assistance in drafting the HHS plan, including guardrails intended to improve safety, such as requiring pharmacies to use peptide ingredients from FDA-registered factories. Additionally, compounders are directed to collect information on side effects for safety analysis and verify the purity of peptides they use. Lurie pointed out that the FDA, under federal law, does not have the authority to enforce those pharmacy requirements. The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding, which represents specialty pharmacies, said several details need to be clarified — including when the policy takes effect and how it will intersect with state pharmacy boards, who traditionally regulate pharmacists. Decisions about regulating peptides and compounding pharmacies have almost always come from the FDA, which has an office dedicated to protecting U.S. consumers from unsafe or poor-quality compounded drugs. The issue of compounding safety became a greater focus for the FDA after a deadly outbreak of fungal meningitis in 2012 was linked to contaminated injections from a Massachusetts compounding pharmacy. Once a niche business, compounding has grown into a multibillion-dollar industry, providing customized medications to doctors, clinics and hospitals. It’s extremely rare for HHS to take the lead in drafting policies over the compounding industry, former FDA officials said. But federal law technically gives HHS authority over drug regulations, which are then delegated to the FDA. Many in the U.S. who are using peptides today do not deal with a doctor or a pharmacy to get the injections, but often order vials online sold by chemical manufacturers based in China. Peptide sellers often try to skirt U.S. regulations by labeling their products as “for research use only” because the FDA does not regulate research chemicals. In 2023, the FDA added more than a dozen peptides , including BPC-157 and TB-500, to its list of substances that should not be compounded due to risks of allergic reactions, kidney damage and tumor growth. At a meeting in July , FDA staffers reiterated that more than half a dozen peptides brought forward for reconsideration remained unproven in terms of safety and effectiveness. But a panel of outside experts voted to drop restrictions on the six peptides named in Wednesday’s document. The panel — selected by Kennedy’s HHS — included several doctors, pharmacists and consultants who work in the peptide field.

title: New study suggests 3 in 4 former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023 had CTE
content: A new study estimates about 3 in 4 former National Football League players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy — an even higher level than identified in another recent study of former players. The new study , published Wednesday in the journal JAMA Network Open, aimed to provide a clearer view of how many former football players have the progressive neurodegenerative disease. CTE has been linked to repetitive head impacts that often occur during contact sports such as football, soccer and hockey. CTE has also been detected in the brains of people who were in the military and exposed to traumatic explosions as well as victims of domestic violence. The brain trauma causes an abnormal buildup of the protein tau, and changes in the brain can begin years before symptoms are detected. CTE can be definitively diagnosed only after death, but it has been associated with symptoms that overlap with dementia such as depression, anxiety, memory loss and lack of impulse control. Previous studies detected the disease in as many as 99% of former NFL players whose brains had been donated for research. However, a significant limitation of these studies was in their potential bias: They were done in a group of people whose brains had been donated by family members who may have noticed symptoms while the person was still alive. A study published in August found that at least 1 in 4 former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE. The study compared data from death certificates to determine the number of former professional players who had died against the number of brain donors confirmed to have CTE. For this new study, Dr. Yorghos Tripodis and other researchers from Boston University’s CTE Center wanted to estimate the prevalence of CTE cases among an even broader group of former professional football players, including those who may not have noticed symptoms or donated their brains for research. The researchers used data from the Understanding Neurologic Injury and Traumatic Encephalopathy brain bank combined with National Death Index records from former NFL players. They included brain donor and nondonor NFL players who died between January 2008 and December 2023. Of 2,362 players who died during that time, 396 had donated their brains for research. Among those, 362 — 93.5% — had been diagnosed with CTE. Almost 70% of the players studied died at the age 70 years or older. The researchers then looked at death certificates for the 2,362 people who died during the time period, finding that former players who had cognitive symptoms related to dementia were five times more likely to have their brains donated. Donations were more likely to come from families of players who had more symptoms or who died at a younger age. The researchers adjusted the rate of disease among those who donated their brains to consider who was most likely to donate and applied that to the broader population of former players. When asked about this newest study, the NFL referred to a statement sent in response to the August study: “The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts. “The NFL remains ​committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust – and expanding – set of resources ​to enhance their physical and mental well being. We encourage former players to utilize these ⁠resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health.” Tripodis said there are limitations to the new research — no study can remove all selection bias and researchers cannot expand the number to populations other than former NFL players. Evidence of CTE in the brain doesn’t mean all players have symptoms. “Our numbers suggest that the prevalence of dementia, which is the most severe type of cognitive symptoms, is four times higher than the general population among the NFL players,” he said. “The symptoms are high, but doesn’t mean that everybody will have symptoms, doesn’t even mean that everybody with symptoms will have the most severe symptoms at the end of their lives.” Dr. Rachel Grashow, a senior research scientist at Harvard University who was not involved in the new research, said the one “tricky” part to the study is understanding why someone donates their brain. She said that if researchers didn’t account for other factors for brain donation, the math “may not be accurate.” It’s important to separate CTE from dementia, she said. CTE refers to the presence of the protein tau in specific regions in the brain and is measured in stages I through IV. Researchers have found higher rates of dementia among those with stages III and IV CTE only. “We want to be careful to say that while there are no diagnostic symptoms linked to all of those found to have CTE at all stages, the ones with relatively the most tau protein aggregation show cognitive symptoms — issues with memory, concentration. Cognitive symptoms are different from mood symptoms — depression and anxiety,” Grashow said in an email. Dr. Julie Stamm, a clinical assistant professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, said she was surprised by the high number of presumed CTE cases found in the study after researchers adjusted for who was most likely to donate their brain. “We talk a lot about the bias of brain banks and how you don’t tend to donate unless you think something’s wrong, and I think that’s been a critique of some of the papers that have come out,” said Stamm, who was not involved with the new research. Stamm said the NFL can go “a lot farther” in regard to safety to encourage earlier levels of the game to do more, such as not tackling in practices. “If the NFL says that, the youth levels, the younger levels, they’ll listen, and that will go a long way in decreasing the overall number of impacts over a lifetime that these individuals sustain, which is what we’ve seen increases the risk for CTE,” Stamm said. Tripodis said that when researchers have a precise estimate of CTE cases from deceased football players, it will motivate them to invest more into research on the disease. “We’re having significant progress of identifying diagnostic criteria for living patients, designing the clinical trials that will find a cure for the disease,” he said.

title: ‘Oil pulling’: Natural, stronger mouthwash or waste of time?
content: Before there was toothpaste, there was coconut oil. Without a toothbrush in hand, many of our ancestors pulled oil between their teeth. The ancient tradition has had a revival. “Oil pulling” is all over the internet. Some of us are posting our routines: digging into a jar of coconut oil, shovel a spoonful into our mouths, and, as it dissolves into a liquid, swishing it through our teeth for five to 20 minutes. Then we spit it out before regular toothbrushing and flossing, repeating the routine several times a week. It’s like natural mouthwash. Some claim oil pulling can make our teeth whiter and freshen our breath. Others claim it promotes a healthier oral microbiome, which connects to better gut health. Oil pulling dates back thousands of years. It’s rooted in Ayurvedic medicine, a traditional Indian healing practice. Influencers’ rendition of oil pulling today is identical to the ancient technique. It involved swishing an edible oil, such as coconut, sunflower or olive, around the mouth for as long as 20 minutes before spitting it out. According to the Ayurvedic practice it was believed the habit would “pull” toxins and impurities from the mouth. Those toxins refer to plaque buildup — a mix of mouth bacteria and leftover food particles that stick to the teeth. Because oral health is linked to overall health, it was also believed that oil pulling could detoxify the body. By the early 20th century, the ancient practice was overtaken by toothpaste, which is medically proven to strengthen oral health. Its recent comeback is part of a larger trend toward natural wellness practices. “There’s no scientific evidence that oil pulling is beneficial, but there is also no evidence that it’s detrimental,” said Dr. Matthew Messina, a consumer advisor for the American Dental Association and director of Ohio State Upper Arlington Dentistry. A 2022 meta-analysis found that oil pulling does decrease bacterial counts in the mouth, but there’s limited evidence that it reduces gum inflammation or plaque buildup compared with the typical hygiene routine. Before we had access to toothpaste, oil pulling was “better than nothing,” Messina said. But now, the long ritual offers little beyond the brushing and flossing habits we learned as kids. There aren’t any “reliable scientific studies to show that oil pulling reduces cavities, whitens teeth or improves oral health and well-being,” according to the American Dental Association. Experts aren’t recommending oil pulling, but they’re not raising any red flags either. Some of Messina’s patients say their mouths taste like a “salad” after oil pulling, so they brush for longer periods of time to get that oily feeling out. “In a backwards way, their oral hygiene actually gets better because they’re brushing longer, which I’m okay with,” he said. “That gets us the same end result.” It’s an issue though, if I’m oil pulling as a replacement for proven medical treatments. For example, if I have a gum infection or dental abscess, I should seek antibiotics, not the unproven healing properties of … oil. And while accidentally swallowing it might cause gastrointestinal problems, that isn’t necessarily harmful. Unlike oil pulling, traditional mouthwash offers some benefits. Mouthwash often contains antibacterial ingredients that reduce bacteria associated with tooth decay and gum disease. Fluoride rinses can help strengthen teeth, Messina said. But mouthwash is still a supplement, not a substitute for brushing and flossing. “Oral rinses are best used to support a healthy regimen of brushing twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between our teeth once a day with floss or an oral irrigator,” Messina said. As for oil pulling, it’s basically a waste of time. You might think you’re spending 20 minutes boosting your oral hygiene, when in reality, you’re probably doing nothing. Oil pulling offers a “false sense of protection,” said dentist and orthodontic specialist Dr. Kami Hoss, who is based near San Diego. While the 2022 study does look at the number of bacteria present after oil pulling, it doesn’t give enough evidence to support oil pulling as beneficial to preventing cavities or periodontal disease. Further study, including more randomized protocols involving a larger number of patients, would be beneficial. “If you spend minutes of oil pulling every day, how much time are you really going to spend doing all the other things that we know are scientific rewards?” Hoss asked. It’s also a waste of perfectly good oil.

A new study reveals a previously overlooked weakness in certain cancer cells that could help researchers refine targeted treatments and reduce harmful side effects. Cancer cells that have lost one safeguard against DNA damage can become dependent on another, an enzyme called Wee1. Drugs that block Wee1 aim to exploit that weakness, but serious side effects are disrupting clinical trials and threatening their adoption in the clinic. One of the cell’s main safeguards is the tumor-suppressor protein p53, which can halt the cell cycle when DNA damage is detected. In around half of all cancers, p53 is inactive, allowing damaged cells to continue growing. Wee1 provides a second line of defense, acting as a backup brake that prevents cells with damaged DNA from entering cell division. Cancers with mutated p53 rely on this remaining safeguard, making Wee1 an attractive drug target. A study published in Nature has now revealed that Wee1 also helps healthy cells begin copying their DNA, much earlier in the cell cycle. Researchers from the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS), the University of Oxford, and UCL found that this role involves a protein degradation complex, a group of proteins that breaks down molecules needed for DNA replication. Wee1 helps switch off the complex so replication can begin. Without Wee1, the complex remains active, delaying or preventing cells from progressing through the cell cycle. “We think what’s happening in patients is that when they’re being treated with these Wee1 inhibitors, it’s stopping their normal fast proliferating cells, like you get in the colon and the blood system, from starting to replicate,” says Alexis, head of the Cell Cycle Control group at the LMS. “And so those cells are stuck, unable to generate new cells, and that could be causing some of the toxic side effects.” The discovery grew out of an effort to test the established understanding of Wee1’s activity early in the cell cycle. The team built a mathematical model based on the scientific literature to predict what would happen when the enzyme was inhibited. “Wee1 has been very intensely studied in the later stages of the cell cycle, where targeting its activity for cancer treatment makes sense,” says Alexis. “However, the side effects of Wee1 inhibitors in patients were hard to explain based on these functions so we started to wonder if this Wee1 enzyme had some other function that we hadn’t appreciated that could explain these. We wanted to look earlier in the cell cycle to see if there was something we had missed.” The researchers then tested the model’s predictions in healthy and cancerous cells. Alexis says, “We quickly found out that the model we had based on the literature on Wee1 was wrong because that was not what we saw in cells. What had been missed was an early function of Wee1 that people hadn’t looked at.” If the side effects are linked to Wee1’s role in controlling the protein degradation complex, the findings could help identify patients most likely to benefit from treatment. The researchers suggest that cancers with reduced activity of this complex may be particularly susceptible to Wee1 inhibitors. That could create a therapeutic window in which lower doses kill cancer cells while limiting damage to healthy cells and reducing side effects. “We’re also starting to think about if there are different ways we could inhibit Wee1 that get round this early cell cycle function,” says Alexis, “though how this might be achieved is a work in progress.” The researchers now want to test the work’s predictions further in preclinical models and in patients currently enrolled in Wee1 inhibitor clinical trials. Those tests could help determine whether the newly identified function explains the toxic effects and how that understanding might guide safer treatment. “Now we’ve uncovered this new function for Wee1, are there other functions that we haven’t appreciated? What else is it doing that we have not seen since we’ve not looked at the right stage?” asks Alexis. Reference: “WEE1 opposes APC/CCDH1 activity to promote S phase entry” by Luc-Alban Vuillemenot, Lucas G. Morales, Calin-Mihai Dragoi, Betheney R. Pennycook, Edward Harris, Liuyang C. Lin, William A. Weston, Jade-Ellen Brown, Emma Graham, Leelou Moulin, Ivan Andrew, Georgia Roumelioti, Alex Montoya, Laurence Game, George R. Young, Keshava K. Datta, Pavel Shliaha, Béla Novák, Hiroyuki Yamano and Alexis R. Barr, 21 October 2026, Nature . DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11188-x This study was funded by the Medical Research Council and Cancer Research UK. Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. A hopeful new direction in the fight against breast cancer may lie in the body’s own defenses, as mouse experiments suggest that protection weakened by obesity could be restored. Breast cancer develops in tissue surrounded by fat cells, and those cells may play a greater role in controlling tumor growth than previously understood. Researchers have discovered that fat cells in lean breast tissue produce a molecule that helps destroy cancerous cells. In obesity, production of this protective molecule drops, potentially removing one of the body’s natural defenses against breast cancer. The finding comes from researchers at Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah (the U), who identified a previously underappreciated way obesity may contribute to breast cancer. Rather than simply creating conditions that encourage cancer growth, obesity may also weaken a biological process that normally helps eliminate dangerous cells. The research was led by Keren Hilgendorf, PhD, a Huntsman Cancer Institute investigator and assistant professor of biochemistry at the U, and first author Meghan Curtin, a doctoral candidate in molecular biology at the university. Their findings were published in the journal Science . Much of the breast consists of fat cells called adipocytes. These cells become larger with obesity, changing the surrounding tissue environment in ways that can affect cancer cells. By studying preclinical models, including breast tissue from donors, the researchers identified a key difference between lean and obese adipocytes involving a fatty acid known as 9S-HODE. Lean adipocytes produced substantially more 9S-HODE than obese adipocytes. This molecule helps promote ferroptosis, a form of cell death involving iron-dependent damage to cellular fats. Ferroptosis is one of the processes through which the body can eliminate old or damaged cells, including those that could become cancerous. “We found that the lean adipocytes produce much more 9S-HODE than obese ones. This means that cancerous cells die more readily in lean tissue,” says Curtin. “By producing more 9S-HODE, our bodies are actively protecting us, under lean circumstances, in a way it cannot with obesity.” The researchers also tested whether restoring this molecule could change tumor growth. In preclinical mouse models, increasing 9S-HODE levels in obese adipocytes suppressed breast cancer tumor growth. This suggests that the reduced production of 9S-HODE associated with obesity may contribute directly to the loss of a protective mechanism. For Hilgendorf, the results offer a different way to understand the relationship between obesity and cancer. “We uncovered the role of a molecule that normally appears in lean tissue that restrains breast cancer growth but is less present with obesity,” says Hilgendorf. “We know obesity is often a driver of breast cancer, and researchers in our field usually consider how obesity is promoting the disease. But we hadn’t really considered that obesity could also be the loss of something that naturally protects us.” That distinction could have implications for treatment. If 9S-HODE helps limit tumor growth, researchers may eventually be able to develop therapies that restore its protective activity. The mouse experiments provide early evidence supporting this possibility, although further research is needed to determine whether the approach could work in patients. “From a clinical perspective, this discovery is incredibly empowering. Because 9S-HODE is naturally present in the body but is lost with obesity, we may be able to restore this protection by putting it back,” says Hilgendorf. “That could become a very feasible therapeutic approach to slow breast cancer growth.” The researchers emphasize that obesity is only one of several factors contributing to breast cancer, which can also develop for unrelated reasons. Their findings suggest that 9S-HODE is produced primarily by fat cells in the breast, although fat cells elsewhere in the body may provide similar protection. Whether this mechanism operates in other tissues remains an open question. “We believe this shift in the understanding of the roles of lean and obese adipocytes is the start of something. This is just one discovery, and it’s not the end of the road,” says Curtin. “This opened our eyes to new ways to think about science, and hopefully we can harness what our bodies are already doing to make progress against this disease.” Reference: “Lean adipocyte oxylipin signaling restrains breast cancer through ferroptosis” by Meghan C. Curtin, Abigail E. Jackson, Mark D. Lee, Elisabeth A. Brown, J. Alan Maschek, David H. Lum, James E. Cox, Alana L. Welm and Keren I. Hilgendorf, 10 September 2026, Science . DOI: 10.1126/science.aea4287 The critical research happening every day at Huntsman Cancer Institute is supported by the National Institutes of Health/National Cancer Institute, including cancer center support grant P30 CA042014, as well as Huntsman Cancer Foundation. A yearlong study of 46 children suggests that brain responses to tempting food images may partly explain the link between ultra-processed diets and increasing body fat. Ultra-processed foods account for about 67% of the daily calories consumed by children in the United States. Although these products have been linked to weight gain and other health problems, scientists are still trying to understand how they may interact with the developing brain. New research suggests that children who eat more ultra-processed foods show stronger brain responses to appetizing food images, and those responses are associated with increases in body fat one year later. Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) include products such as certain breakfast cereals, packaged breads, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and shelf-stable, often containing artificial sweeteners, colors, and other ingredients not typically used in home cooking. Previous studies have linked UPF consumption to weight gain, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, but the role of the brain’s reward system in these associations remains unclear. Childhood may be an especially important time to investigate this relationship because the brain is still developing and food preferences are taking shape. “Children’s brains are still developing, habits are still forming, and food preferences are still being made. It’s an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment,” said study senior author Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. “We’re particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference.” To explore how UPF consumption relates to brain activity and weight gain, researchers studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the long-term BrainChild study , which investigates diabetes and obesity risk. All participants began at a healthy weight, allowing the team to examine potential early signs of increased risk. At the beginning of the study, researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to monitor the children’s brain activity while they viewed pictures of appealing foods, including cookies and French fries. The team also collected information about each child’s diet, body mass index (BMI), body fat percentage, and waist circumference. BMI is a measurement based on height and weight. One year later, researchers measured BMI, body fat percentage, and waist circumference again. The brain scans revealed that children who consumed more UPFs had stronger responses to food pictures in the dorsal striatum, a brain region involved in reward and motivation. Children with stronger responses in this region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the following year. By the end of the study, children who had consumed more UPFs also had higher BMI, body fat percentage, and waist circumference. The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help explain these relationships. When they statistically accounted for how strongly each child’s dorsal striatum responded to food images, the association between UPF consumption and BMI weakened by 31%. The association with body fat percentage weakened by 44%. These findings suggest that the brain’s sensitivity to appealing food cues may help explain part of the relationship between UPF consumption and changes in body composition. “This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain,” Page said. “It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time.” The findings, published in JAMA Network Open , provide evidence of a possible connection between diet, reward-related brain activity, and subsequent changes in body fat. The research was funded in part by the National Institutes of Health. However, because the study was observational, it cannot establish that eating UPFs directly changes brain activity or causes weight gain. The results also do not determine whether stronger brain responses lead children to consume more UPFs or whether their diets influence how the brain responds to food. To investigate cause and effect, Page hopes to conduct an intervention study in which children who regularly consume UPFs are provided with more minimally processed foods. Researchers could then examine whether changing their diets alters their brain responses to food images over time and whether those changes are associated with less weight gain. The researchers also emphasize that improving children’s diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed foods are often among the most affordable, convenient, and accessible options, making dietary changes difficult without broader improvements in food availability. “Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution,” Page said. Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue following participants through puberty and into young adulthood. By tracking changes in brain activity, body composition, diet, and overall health, researchers hope to better understand how eating habits during childhood relate to health later in life. Reference: “Ultraprocessed Food Intake, Striatal Response to Food Cues, and Adiposity Gain in Children” by Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, Jared Smith, Ting Chow, Kay Jann, Anny H. Xiang and Kathleen A. Page, , JAMA Network Open . DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.40252 This research was supported by an American Diabetes Association Pathway Accelerator Award [1-14-ACE-36]; the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) [R01DK116858, R01DK134079]. The REDCap database used for this study was supported by the Southern California Clinical and Translational Science Institute [NIH UL1TR001855].
